transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

I came in because I’m really not functioning at work the way I need to. I’m a physical scientist, and normally I can hold a whole experiment in my head — the setup, the timing, what needs to be checked, what can wait — but lately I just can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment.

Like, I’ll be on a grant call, or in a safety meeting where I’m supposed to be listening and making decisions, and suddenly I’ll notice something completely off to the side — a pump vibrating in a slightly weird rhythm, or a student making some small comment, or I’ll remember some odd peak from an old spectrum that probably isn’t even relevant — and then I’m gone. Not physically gone, but my mind is off chasing that one thing for hours. I’ll start pulling files or checking equipment or mentally redesigning the whole analysis, and meanwhile the thing everyone actually needed from me just sort of falls apart.

It’s embarrassing, honestly, because these are not little low-stakes things. People are waiting on me, and I know what I’m supposed to be doing, but it’s like every stray detail becomes urgent and fascinating, and I can’t stay with the main task. That’s what finally made me come in.
Can you tell me if this kind of difficulty staying focused has happened before in your life, or if it’s something that’s mostly started recently, especially in relation to any stress or mood changes?

It’s mostly been recent, at least at this level. I mean, I’ve always been someone who can get interested in side details — that’s part of science, sometimes it’s useful — but this kind of losing the thread and not being able to pull myself back has been going on for about seven months.

It really started after I took over this multi-site spectroscopy project. That’s when it became noticeable, because there were suddenly so many moving parts and so many people depending on me to keep the main line of work organized. Since then, the focus problem has just been… persistent. Not a bad week here or there, but months of it. Seven months, roughly.

When you get deeply involved in one of those interesting details — like an odd peak in a spectrum or a technical puzzle — do you sometimes get so absorbed in it that you lose track of time or forget about other things you were supposed to do?

Yes. Very much so. It’s not just that I get interested and then come back five minutes later — I’ll think I’m just going to check one thing, like why a pump sounds a little off or whether some old spectral peak connects to what we’re seeing now, and then suddenly I’ve spent hours following that thread.

And the whole time it feels important, like I’m on the verge of solving something, so I don’t register that I’ve stopped doing the actual thing I was supposed to be doing. I’ll be in a grant call or a safety meeting, and I’m supposed to be tracking decisions or answering people, but some side detail grabs me and I’m mentally somewhere else. Then afterward I realize people were waiting on me, or the main experiment needed attention, and I let that slip because I was off chasing the interesting detail. It’s really disruptive.
When you get deeply involved in one of these details, do you lose track of time or become unaware of what's going on around you, almost like you're in a different world?

Yes — that’s exactly what it feels like. Not like I’m unconscious of the room, but it’s like the room stops being the main thing. I’ll still be sitting there in the grant call or the safety meeting, but some tiny detail hooks me — the rhythm of a pump vibrating, or something a student says under their breath, or I’ll remember an odd peak from an old spectrum — and suddenly that becomes the whole world.

And I don’t mean I just think, “Oh, interesting,” and then go back to the meeting. I mean I’m off. I start mentally following it, making connections, thinking about files I should pull, equipment I should check, whether it changes the experiment design, whether everyone missed something important. It can go on for hours, and during that time I’m not really tracking what people are asking me or what the experiment actually needs right then.

Then I come back to myself and realize the thing everyone needed from me has sort of fallen apart while I was chasing this one detail. It’s embarrassing because I know I’m supposed to be responsible for the main experiment, but in those moments the side detail feels urgent and fascinating, like I can’t let it go.

When you’re not in a meeting or during an experiment, do you also find yourself getting completely absorbed in other tasks — like reading, tinkering with equipment, or even just thinking about a problem — to the point where you might lose track of time or forget about other things you meant to do?

Yes. It’s not only in meetings or when the experiment is actively running. If I’m at my desk, or in the lab after everyone’s gone, or even just sitting with a notebook thinking through something, I can disappear into it for hours.

It usually starts very small. I’ll mean to look up one old spectrum, or check whether a pump vibration pattern matches something from a previous setup, or follow up on some side comment a student made earlier. And then it just… expands. One file leads to another file, then I’m sketching possible explanations, then I’m thinking, “Wait, if that’s true, the whole way we’re interpreting this run might be wrong,” and suddenly the original task — the actual experiment, the thing I was supposed to keep organized — is completely gone from my mind.

That’s really why I came in. I can’t reliably keep my mind on the main line of work anymore. I’ll be chasing this fascinating detail, and while I’m doing that, the thing everyone needs from me just falls apart or gets neglected. It feels compelling in the moment, like I’m doing the most important thing, but afterward I realize I’ve lost hours and missed what I actually meant to do.

When you get absorbed in one of these interesting details, do you ever fail to notice that you’ve completely stopped working on your main task — like not realizing you haven’t responded to questions, missed key decisions, or left people hanging — until someone points it out to you afterward?

Yes. That’s actually one of the scariest parts of it, because I don’t always realize in the moment that I’ve stopped doing the actual thing I’m there to do.

Like in a grant call, I’ll be physically present, I’ll have the document open, people will be talking through decisions, and then something tiny will catch me — a phrase someone uses, or some technical inconsistency, or I’ll suddenly remember an odd peak from an older spectrum that might relate. And I’ll think I’m just holding that thought for a second, but I’m not. I’m gone into it. I start building this whole chain in my head: what file I need to check, whether that peak showed up before, whether the pump noise we heard last week means something, whether we’ve been interpreting the experiment wrong.

And while I’m doing that, I don’t notice that someone asked me a question or that the group is waiting for me to weigh in. Sometimes I only realize because there’s this pause and someone says my name again, or afterward a student will tell me, “We needed you to decide that,” and I have this awful sinking feeling because I genuinely didn’t register that I’d left them hanging.

It happens in safety meetings too, or around the experiment itself. I’ll notice a pump vibration or a side comment from a student, and suddenly I’m chasing that thread like it’s the most important thing in the world. Then later I realize the main task — the thing everyone actually needed from me — has fallen apart or been neglected because I was absorbed in this detail. That’s really why I came in. I can’t keep my mind on the actual experiment anymore.
When you get absorbed in these details, do you find it extremely difficult to pull yourself away, even if you know you should, because it feels so intensely engaging or stimulating?

Yes. Extremely difficult. That’s the part that makes it feel less like normal curiosity and more like I’ve been grabbed by something.

I can know, at some level, that I should stop — like I can know I’m in a grant call and people are waiting, or that the safety meeting has moved on, or that the actual experiment needs decisions from me — but the detail feels so alive that pulling away feels almost impossible. A pump vibration will catch me, or a student will make some small comment, or I’ll remember an odd peak from an old spectrum, and it’s like my mind says, “No, this is the real thing, follow this.” And then I’m chasing it.

And it’s not just a passing thought. It feels urgent and stimulating, like there’s something important hidden in it and if I let go I’ll lose the thread. So I keep going — mentally, or actually opening files, sketching notes, comparing things — and hours can go by. Meanwhile the thing I’m supposed to be responsible for is just… not getting done. People need me to stay on the main experiment, and instead I’m locked onto this one piece of it until everything else starts falling apart.

That’s really why I came in. It isn’t that I don’t care about the main work. I do. But once one of these details hooks me, I have a very hard time making myself come back.

Have you noticed any changes in your mood, like feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or on the flip side, feeling unusually energetic, irritable, or restless during this time?

Yes… yes, definitely. I wouldn’t say it’s been “down” exactly — not mostly. It’s more the other side of it. For months now I’ve felt like the lab is finally moving at my speed, if that makes sense. Like everything is charged, almost electrified, and I can see connections faster than everyone else can keep up with.

At first it felt wonderful, honestly. Like, finally, the work has momentum, finally I can see what needs to happen, finally the whole place is catching up to the pace I’ve always felt it should have. But then when someone questions my plan, or asks me to slow down, or wants another meeting before we act, I get… I snap. Much more sharply than I mean to.

It’s embarrassing to say, but students have started avoiding my office. I can tell. They hesitate outside the door, or they email instead of coming in, and I know it’s because if they push back or ask me to explain something again, I might bite their head off. In the moment it feels like they’re obstructing something obvious and urgent, but afterward I realize I was too harsh. It’s not how I want to be with them.
Have you found yourself needing less sleep lately, or having trouble sleeping because your mind is racing or you feel too energized to rest?

Yes. Very much. That’s been happening most nights now. I’ll sleep maybe two or three hours, sometimes not even properly in bed — I’ll end up on the couch with my laptop still open, like I only meant to check one more thing and then suddenly it’s morning.

But the strange thing is, I don’t wake up feeling ruined the way I should. I wake up sharp. Like my head is already switched on before I’m fully awake. I’ll come to and immediately know what file I want to open, what calculation I want to rerun, what note I need to send. It doesn’t feel like, “Oh God, I barely slept.” It feels more like sleep was this inconvenient interruption that I had to tolerate for a couple of hours.

And I know that sounds bad when I say it out loud. Normally, if I slept that little, I’d expect to be dragging or useless. But lately it’s almost the opposite — lying down feels inefficient, like I’m wasting time when my mind is already moving. So I’ll tell myself I should go to bed, and then I just… don’t, or I do for a little while and then I’m up again, ready to work.
Have you experienced any distinct periods where your mood was unusually high, elevated, or irritable to the point where it was noticeably different from your usual self?

Yes. I mean… yes, very clearly. It’s been noticeably different from how I usually am.

For months I’ve had this feeling that the lab is finally moving at my speed — like everything is almost electrified, like I can see what needs to happen and I’m pushing everyone toward it because it all feels so obvious and urgent to me. It’s not just being in a good mood. It’s more intense than that. There’s this charged quality to it, like the whole place should be accelerating and I’m the only one who really understands the pace it needs.

And then the irritable part is… honestly, that’s been the most visible. If someone questions my plan, or asks me to slow down, or wants to go back over something I feel we already settled, I snap. Not just a little impatient — I get sharp, cutting. In the moment it feels like they’re blocking something important, but afterward I can see I reacted way out of proportion.

It’s gotten to the point where students avoid coming into my office. I’ve noticed them hesitating at the door, or sending emails instead of just asking me something directly, and I hate that. I don’t want to be someone they’re afraid to approach. But yes — this has been a distinct shift. I don’t feel like my usual self.

I can know, at some level, that I should stop — like I can know I’m in a grant call and people are waiting, or that the safety meeting has moved on, or that the actual experiment needs decisions from me — but the detail feels so alive that pulling away feels almost impossible. A pump vibration will catch me, or a student will make some small comment, or I’ll remember an odd peak from an old spectrum, and it’s like my mind says, “No, this is the real thing, follow this.” And then I’m chasing it.

And it’s not just a passing thought. It feels urgent and stimulating, like there’s something important hidden in it and if I let go I’ll lose the thread. So I keep going — mentally, or actually opening files, sketching notes, comparing things — and hours can go by. Meanwhile the thing I’m supposed to be responsible for is just… not getting done. People need me to stay on the main experiment, and instead I’m locked onto this one piece of it until everything else starts falling apart.

That’s really why I came in. It isn’t that I don’t care about the main work. I do. But once one of these details hooks me, I have a very hard time making myself come back.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of mood disturbance (e.g., depression or mania) that may suggest a mood disorder (e.g., major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder) as a contributor to their current difficulties.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your mood, like feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, or on the flip side, feeling unusually energetic, irritable, or restless during this time?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For months I've felt like the lab is finally moving at my speed, almost electrified, but if someone questions my plan or asks me to slow down I snap at them in a way that has made students avoid my office.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about mood changes during this period, especially feeling unusually energetic, irritable, or restless; the profile item that most directly covers the mood component is elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, definitely. I wouldn’t say it’s been “down” exactly — not mostly. It’s more the other side of it. For months now I’ve felt like the lab is finally moving at my speed, if that makes sense. Like everything is charged, almost electrified, and I can see connections faster than everyone else can keep up with.

At first it felt wonderful, honestly. Like, finally, the work has momentum, finally I can see what needs to happen, finally the whole place is catching up to the pace I’ve always felt it should have. But then when someone questions my plan, or asks me to slow down, or wants another meeting before we act, I get… I snap. Much more sharply than I mean to.

It’s embarrassing to say, but students have started avoiding my office. I can tell. They hesitate outside the door, or they email instead of coming in, and I know it’s because if they push back or ask me to explain something again, I might bite their head off. In the moment it feels like they’re obstructing something obvious and urgent, but afterward I realize I was too harsh. It’s not how I want to be with them.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's irritability and snapping at others has been accompanied by a decreased need for sleep or insomnia, which would help differentiate between bipolar disorder (e.g., F33.0, F33.1, F33.2) and other conditions like ADHD or OCD.
doctor.question: Have you found yourself needing less sleep lately, or having trouble sleeping because your mind is racing or you feel too energized to rest?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: Most nights I sleep two or three hours, sometimes on the couch with my laptop open, and I wake up sharp and ready to work instead of tired, like sleep is an inefficient interruption.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether I need less sleep or feel too energized/racing to rest, which matches decreased need for sleep.

patient.answer:
Yes. Very much. That’s been happening most nights now. I’ll sleep maybe two or three hours, sometimes not even properly in bed — I’ll end up on the couch with my laptop still open, like I only meant to check one more thing and then suddenly it’s morning.

But the strange thing is, I don’t wake up feeling ruined the way I should. I wake up sharp. Like my head is already switched on before I’m fully awake. I’ll come to and immediately know what file I want to open, what calculation I want to rerun, what note I need to send. It doesn’t feel like, “Oh God, I barely slept.” It feels more like sleep was this inconvenient interruption that I had to tolerate for a couple of hours.

And I know that sounds bad when I say it out loud. Normally, if I slept that little, I’d expect to be dragging or useless. But lately it’s almost the opposite — lying down feels inefficient, like I’m wasting time when my mind is already moving. So I’ll tell myself I should go to bed, and then I just… don’t, or I do for a little while and then I’m up again, ready to work.

inference.note: This turn added F31.81 (Bipolar II disorder) and F30.1 (Manic episode, moderate) due to the presence of elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and irritability, which are indicative of a manic episode. F33.2 (Recurrent depressive disorder, current episode severe) remains as a candidate due to the irritability and potential overlap with mixed features, but the predominant clinical picture now suggests a bipolar spectrum disorder. No other major conditions were ruled out.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood that represents a noticeable change from their usual behavior, which would help differentiate between bipolar I disorder (current manic episode) and other candidates.
doctor.question: Have you experienced any distinct periods where your mood was unusually high, elevated, or irritable to the point where it was noticeably different from your usual self?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For months I've felt like the lab is finally moving at my speed, almost electrified, but if someone questions my plan or asks me to slow down I snap at them in a way that has made students avoid my office.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking about distinct periods of unusually elevated or irritable mood that are noticeably different from usual self.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… yes, very clearly. It’s been noticeably different from how I usually am.

For months I’ve had this feeling that the lab is finally moving at my speed — like everything is almost electrified, like I can see what needs to happen and I’m pushing everyone toward it because it all feels so obvious and urgent to me. It’s not just being in a good mood. It’s more intense than that. There’s this charged quality to it, like the whole place should be accelerating and I’m the only one who really understands the pace it needs.

And then the irritable part is… honestly, that’s been the most visible. If someone questions my plan, or asks me to slow down, or wants to go back over something I feel we already settled, I snap. Not just a little impatient — I get sharp, cutting. In the moment it feels like they’re blocking something important, but afterward I can see I reacted way out of proportion.

It’s gotten to the point where students avoid coming into my office. I’ve noticed them hesitating at the door, or sending emails instead of just asking me something directly, and I hate that. I don’t want to be someone they’re afraid to approach. But yes — this has been a distinct shift. I don’t feel like my usual self.

inference.note: The patient has described symptoms consistent with a manic episode, including elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and impaired judgment. These symptoms point to a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder, most recent episode manic. The other candidates (F30.1 and F33.2) are ruled out as the patient has clearly described a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated mood, which is required for F31.x codes rather than unipolar depression (F32.x/F33.x) or a single manic episode not part of a recurrent disorder (F30.x).
